name: Asthma in children: signs and NHS advice
summary: Parents may notice wheezing, cough or a tight chest; diagnosis can take time, and the NHS says call 999 if the reliever is not helping.
keyPoints: The NHS lists wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness as the main signs of asthma, and they usually come and go.
Diagnosis can take time because symptoms vary, and testing is difficult in young children, so a trial of asthma medicines may be used.
Reliever inhalers are used when needed and preventer inhalers every day; children who use an inhaler are advised to use a spacer.
Every child with asthma should have a written asthma action plan and a review at least once a year.
Call 999 for an asthma attack that the reliever inhaler does not control; contact the GP the same day when symptoms are worsening.

body.heading: What does asthma look like in a child?
body.body: Asthma is a common long-term condition in which the airways are inflamed and sensitive. The NHS lists wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and chest tightness as the main signs, and they often flare at night or early in the morning. Wheezing is a whistling sound when a child breathes, and a dry cough that does not go away, especially at night or after exercise, is also on the NHS list. Asthma and Lung UK says younger children may complain of a tummy ache, lose their appetite, say their ribs ache or seem more tired than usual. The NHS says these symptoms usually come and go. Asthma and Lung UK suggests a visit to the GP if a child needs the blue reliever inhaler three or more times a week, wakes at night coughing or wheezing, struggles with exercise, or misses school because of asthma.

body.heading: How is asthma diagnosed in children, and why can it take time?
body.body: The NHS says a GP or nurse usually asks questions and listens to the chest. A simple breathing test may also be used, and the NHS names spirometry and peak flow tests as the main ones. Asthma can take time to diagnose because the symptoms often change over time. Guidance used by the NHS says a diagnosis should be confirmed once a child is able to manage lung function tests. In children under 5, that testing is difficult, and spirometry is not practical for this age group. Wheezing is common in many other chest conditions, and most children whose wheezing comes with viral infections stop wheezing as they get older and do not develop asthma. For young children who cannot do lung function tests, a clinician may suggest a trial of asthma medicines. NICE guidance, written with the British Thoracic Society and SIGN, describes this trial as part of reaching a diagnosis, with a review afterwards to see whether symptoms return. The pathway also notes that getting better on treatment is not proof of asthma, because wheezing caused by a virus can settle on its own.

body.heading: What can trigger asthma in a child?
body.body: A trigger is something that makes asthma symptoms flare up. Asthma and Lung UK lists colds and viruses, exercise, weather changes, smoke and pollution, strong emotions, and allergens such as pollen, dust mites, pets or mould. It describes colds and viruses as the most common cause of flare-ups. Every child has their own set of triggers, and it helps to record them in the asthma plan. Keeping a diary of symptoms and triggers, in a notebook or on a phone, can help families spot them. The NHS says there is not currently enough evidence to know whether suspected causes such as genetics and pollution actually cause asthma.

body.heading: What treatment do children with asthma get?
body.body: The NHS says inhalers are the mainstay of treatment, with tablets or other treatments used if inhalers are not enough. A reliever inhaler is used when needed to relieve symptoms quickly for a short time. A preventer inhaler is used every day to stop symptoms happening. Asthma and Lung UK says the preventer is used daily as prescribed, even when a child feels well. One NHS page says a child who uses the reliever often will also need a preventer inhaler. Children who use a metered-dose inhaler are advised to use a spacer, a device that helps the medicine get into the lungs. Younger children may be given their medicine through a nebuliser instead of an inhaler.

body.heading: What are an asthma action plan and an annual review?
body.body: An asthma action plan is a written guide made with the GP or asthma nurse. It explains how to look after the child's asthma every day and what to do if symptoms get worse. Asthma and Lung UK says every child with asthma should have one, covering daily medicines, triggers, symptoms and what to do in an attack. Many plans use green, amber and red zones. Asthma and Lung UK suggests sharing the plan with the child's school or college. The NHS says a personal plan should be reviewed with a nurse, doctor or pharmacist at least once a year. Asthma and Lung UK says a child should have an asthma review at least once a year, and the GP surgery usually sends an invitation. At the review the GP or nurse typically asks about symptoms and triggers, checks how often the reliever is used, checks inhaler technique and updates the plan. Families do not need to wait for the review if they are worried, and can speak to the GP, nurse or pharmacist at any time.

body.heading: How can parents recognise an asthma attack?
body.body: The NHS says signs of an attack include symptoms getting worse, the reliever not helping, and being too breathless to speak, eat or sleep. NHS children's pages describe a child who is too breathless to talk, eat or drink, has blue lips, or is very drowsy as an emergency. Asthma and Lung UK says to call 999 if a child's reliever inhaler is not helping their symptoms or is not available. The NHS says to call 999 for an ambulance if the person feels worse at any point, or does not improve after following the attack steps. While waiting, the advice is to keep the child sitting up and calm, and to use a spacer with the inhaler if they have one. Some inhalers, known as MART inhalers, have different attack steps, so the child's own action plan applies.

body.heading: When should parents contact the GP, NHS 111 or 999?
body.body: Call 999 for an attack that the reliever inhaler does not control, or when a child cannot talk, eat or drink because of breathlessness. If a child is wheezy and breathless and the reliever does not keep symptoms away for as long as the action plan expects, local NHS guidance advises contacting the GP the same day. NHS 111 can give urgent advice when the GP surgery is closed. After an attack that led to hospital care, NHS guidance says to arrange a GP appointment within 48 hours of discharge. For symptoms that are more frequent but not urgent, a routine appointment with the GP or asthma nurse is the usual route.
